title: I Posted the Soap-Vat Pour Hours After They Left My Numbered Molds

parts.text: I stepped into the soap studio at 10:03 a.m. and mentor Prue was already using numbered gear. The board said: ONE VAT. NINETY MINUTES. MOLDS STAY WITH THE SLOT. I was thirty, studio secretary, holding a checkout that listed our numbered molds. Prue shrugged. "Mentors are the vat." I photographed the board, the booking, and her leftover lye pitcher on my numbered molds. Then I asked for the pour log. At 10:11 the desk pinged why Prue's name was on my pitcher. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The desk can see Prue's leftover lye pitcher on my numbered molds.

social.video_title: They left my numbered soap molds on my vat hours — Part 1/2
social.description: Soap studio, leftover lye pitcher, a ninety-minute clock she posted. I logged the pour. Would you have asked for the pour log?

parts.text: Prue called it trace until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the pitcher still. The molds went back to my numbered slot. Prue ran a slot of her own and told the next mentor atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: MENTORS ARE NOT THE VAT. I keep my molds on a labeled rack. Prue brown-bags her trace. The studio finally looks like a slot, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Mentors are not the vat — Part 2/2
social.description: Pour log, numbered molds, and a second line on the board. Was trace ever my pitcher?
